clue.text: Open lock possibly underhand?

parts.note: read as 'under hand': a straight is a poker hand, and in a down clue the lock's word sits under it
a lock is a rugby forward, one example of the position, hence 'possibly'

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether picking a lock is somehow a sneaky, underhand business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'underhand' looks like one word meaning sneaky; split it as 'under hand' and, in a down clue, the forward sits beneath the poker hand. A lock is a second-row rugby player.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone open is frank and candid, the synonym meaning honest and direct in dealings.

clue.text: A place for learning in class cut — for our misspelling?

indicators.note: the letters for 'A place for learning' go inside the shortened class word
the class word is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: a grade is a class or rank
a uni, short for university, is a place for learning

explanation.surface: A question about a college place in a class being cut, wondering if that explains a typo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'our' is the Guardian speaking: Private Eye mocked the paper's frequent typos by calling it this, so the clue asks for the paper's name as misspelt.
explanation.definitionFit: Private Eye's jokey nickname for the Guardian mocks its famed typos, so the paper's own name misspelt is this.

clue.text: Match a shade short

indicators.note: the colour word is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: green is a shade, a colour

explanation.surface: A paint-matching task where the colour comes out a shade off.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things match when they correspond or tally, the verb sense of concur or tally.

clue.text: Battle wound acquires bandages

indicators.note: the acquiring word wraps around the wound word as a bandage wraps a wound

parts.note: to acquire something is to have it
a sting is a small wound, from a wasp or bee

explanation.surface: A battlefield injury picks up dressings.
explanation.definitionFit: The Battle of Hastings in 1066 is the famous English battle of the Norman conquest.

clue.text: Bargain, 50% off price to get hold of jalopy

indicators.note: the halved price word grips the jalopy word between its letters
only half of the price word is kept, its first two of four letters

parts.note: the cost of something is its price
a heap is slang for an old, battered car, a jalopy

explanation.surface: A car-dealer's offer: half price on a rundown old banger.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheapo item is inexpensive, used as an adjective for a cut-price bargain.

clue.text: Just one militant maintaining lead in primaries

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the militant word holds up the extra letter inside it

parts.note: martial means warlike, militant

indicators.note: the lead in a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Political primaries in which only one militant candidate keeps the lead.
explanation.walkthrough: P goes inside MARTIAL, after its M.
explanation.definitionFit: Just as an adjective means fair and even-handed, a synonym for unbiased.

clue.text: Time to plug in dry old music player

indicators.note: the time letter plugs into the dry word like a stopper

parts.note: sere means dry or withered

explanation.surface: Time to plug in that old music player, dry as it is.
explanation.definitionFit: A stereo is a hi-fi system, a set that plays recorded sound.

clue.text: Standard inside edges in Melbourne getting team out, error unfortunately inspiring paceman initially

indicators.note: to inspire is to breathe in, so the jumble takes the extra letter inside
things gone unfortunately are in a mess, so these letters are rearranged
the edges in a word are its first and last letters
initially picks the opening letter

explanation.surface: A cricket report: in Melbourne a team is out after an unfortunate error by the fast bowler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'edges' (ME), 'team out' and 'error' are mixed together ('unfortunately'), then 'inspiring' takes in P from 'paceman initially'. 'getting' is only a link. A paceman is a fast bowler in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the normal temperature of an indoor space, the standard warmth expected inside a house.

clue.text: Encapsulating the ultimate in pomposity, standard rubbish from the right — here, primarily?

definitions.text: Encapsulating the ultimate in pomposity, standard rubbish from the right — here, primarily?

indicators.note: the reversed words enclose the extra letter as a capsule encloses its contents
reading from the right means the pair of words is read backwards

parts.note: par is the standard score
grot is slang for rubbish or dirt

indicators.note: the ultimate in a word is its final letter
primarily picks the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A jibe at a pompous right-wing paper full of standard rubbish, as called here at the Guardian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'here' is the Guardian, whose readers coined this nickname for the right-leaning Daily Telegraph, so the whole clue doubles as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the Guardian's mocking nickname for the Daily Telegraph, a pompous Conservative-leaning paper.

clue.text: Too much in flash slogan

indicators.note: the too-much letters go inside the flash word

parts.note: a mo, short for moment, is a flash or instant
OTT is short for over the top, too much

explanation.surface: An advertising slogan that has too much flash about it.
explanation.definitionFit: A motto is a short guiding phrase, a synonym for a slogan.

clue.text: Most keen to put a copper on trial

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
a test is a trial

explanation.surface: An eager police force putting one of its officers on trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a police officer; it is the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Acute means sharp or keen, so the superlative is the keenest, sharpest.

clue.text: Honest sight is 14 20

parts.note: the letters of 'honest sight' rearrange to spell 'those things', so the phrase is a word puzzle of the kind 14/20 names

explanation.walkthrough: '14 20' means the answer to 14/20. 'Honest sight' is literally made of the letters of THOSE THINGS, so it is one of those things: a rearranged phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A word or phrase made from another's letters rearranged; 'honest sight' is such a rearrangement of 'those things'.

clue.text: See 23
Choice from over there? It can't be helped

definitions.meaning: picking a single item from a group over there; the question mark marks the playful literal reading
a resigned phrase for bad luck nobody could avoid

explanation.definitionFit: Said with a shrug, the phrase means an unlucky event was unavoidable; literally, it picks one item from a group.

clue.text: West possibly observing struggle in Balkan city

indicators.note: the struggle word goes inside the city name

parts.note: Mostar is a city in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Balkans
to vie is to compete or struggle

explanation.surface: Someone from the West watching a conflict in a Balkan city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West' looks like the compass point; it is Mae West, the Hollywood actress.
explanation.definitionFit: Mae West was a celebrated Hollywood actress, so she is an example of a screen celebrity.

clue.text: Dull and grey outside in a storm

indicators.note: a storm throws things about, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Grey and dull weather out of doors during a storm.
explanation.definitionFit: Boring and dreary things are dull and grey, the synonym for wearisome and monotonous.

clue.text: Cut uniform with cap

parts.note: flat means uniform or even, as a flat rate
a cap is the top of something

explanation.surface: Trimming a uniform and adding a cap to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like a verb; it is a haircut.
explanation.definitionFit: A haircut with the hair cropped short and level on top, an example of a style of cut.

clue.text: Shabby swimmer lagging behind

indicators.note: lagging is insulating wrap, so the swimmer word wraps around the behind word

parts.note: a fish is a swimmer
the rump is the behind, the backside

explanation.surface: A tatty swimmer falling behind the rest in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lagging behind' reads as trailing; 'lagging' means wrapping, as pipes are lagged.
explanation.definitionFit: Dowdy and old-fashioned in dress, a shabby look; the sense of dowdy is a close synonym.

clue.text: Edit it and change instruction

indicators.note: to edit is to alter and rework, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: An editor's order to edit something and change it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edit' here is the anagram signal on 'it' and 'change'.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving lessons is instruction, the synonym for education or tuition.

clue.text: Missing starter, brush up on very meaty dish

indicators.note: in an across clue, 'up on very' puts up after very
the brush word loses its first letter

parts.note: a fox's tail is called its brush
so means very, as in so good

explanation.surface: A cook skipping the first course and brushing up on a hearty meat dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starter' looks like a first course; it is the first letter, of FOXTAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A rich, beefy broth made from cattle tails, an example of a meaty dish.

clue.text: See 14
A number of numbers written up, three quatrains and a couplet?

indicators.note: in a down clue, written up means the letters are read from the bottom

parts.note: ten is a number

explanation.surface: A poem described as a set of numbers, with its form spelt out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'numbers' also means verses, which fits the poem in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Fourteen lines of three four-line stanzas then a rhyming pair is the Shakespearean form of this poem.

clue.text: Salmon, royal survivor of the sixteenth century?

definitions.meaning: a young salmon in its first stage in fresh water

definitions.text: royal survivor of the sixteenth century?
definitions.meaning: Catherine, sixth wife of Henry VIII, who outlived him

explanation.definitionFit: A juvenile salmon has this name; Henry VIII's last queen, who outlived him, also bore it.

clue.text: General practitioner worried about current network

indicators.note: about means around or every which way, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: GP stands for general practitioner, a family doctor

explanation.surface: A family doctor fretting about something.
explanation.definitionFit: The national network of cables carrying electric current is this, the electricity supply system.

clue.text: Religious festival a jot warmer

parts.note: a whit is a jot, a tiny amount
the sun warms us, so it is a warmer

explanation.surface: A religious festival that is a touch warmer than usual.
explanation.definitionFit: Pentecost is called Whit Sunday in Britain, the Christian feast seven weeks after Easter.

clue.text: Reportedly return as Jeremiah, perhaps?

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said aloud, so the word sounds like the return word

parts.note: profit is a return on investment

explanation.surface: A financial return that comes out as a gloomy Jeremiah.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jeremiah' also means a pessimist, which the surface leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeremiah was an Old Testament seer, an example of a biblical foreteller.

clue.text: Endless trouble recalled about a relative of hip hop

indicators.note: the reversed word goes around the letter a
recalled means called back, so the shortened word is read backwards
the trouble word loses its last letter

parts.note: aggro is British slang for trouble or aggression

explanation.surface: Endless trouble remembered around a music style close to hip hop.
explanation.walkthrough: AGGR read backwards is RGGA; A goes in after the R.
explanation.definitionFit: A Jamaican dance music style mixing reggae and rap, so a close cousin of hip hop.

clue.text: For example, Georgian monarch welcoming a novelist from Ireland

indicators.note: the monarch's letters welcome the others in between them

parts.note: ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
Laurence Sterne, author of Tristram Shandy, was born in Ireland

explanation.surface: A Georgian king hosting an Irish novelist, as in the Georgian era.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Georgian' suggests the British era of the Georges; it is someone from Georgia in eastern Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from Georgia, in the Caucasus, comes from the east of Europe, an example of an eastern inhabitant.
